\citet{zhao2024analysing} showed that residual stream representations carry linearly detectable conflict signals in English, and \citet{brink2026probing} performed knowledge attribution probing to localize factual associations within model parameters.
Extending these approaches cross-lingually introduces additional challenges.
Translation quality may confound probe transfer: a poor translation could alter conflict detection for reasons unrelated to the conflict signal itself.
Token overlap between languages, even when minimal, could provide a shortcut for cross-lingual probes.
Observed asymmetries in transfer accuracy may reflect general cross-lingual properties rather than conflict-specific phenomena, and disentangling these sources requires careful baseline comparisons.
Beyond detectability, a fundamental limitation of probing is that it establishes correlation, not causation \citep{hewitt2019designing}.
\citet{basu2026interpretability} demonstrated that even near-perfect probe accuracy does not guarantee that the detected direction can steer model behavior.

We address these questions through a pipeline that combines residual stream probing with representation steering across three models of distinct architectures: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-2-9B-IT.

XNLI entailment-versus-contradiction probes \citep{conneau2018xnli} show the same directional pattern at comparable magnitude (+6.0, +6.7, and +7.8 pp), with substantially overlapping confidence intervals.
The conflict asymmetry thus parallels a general property of English-dominant models, where Chinese representations project more readily onto English representational space than the reverse.

To ensure these findings are robust, we apply a confound exclusion pipeline that includes COMET-based translation quality stratification, token overlap analysis, and non-conflict baseline comparison.

\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig1_pipeline.pdf}
\caption{Overview of the cross-lingual conflict probing pipeline. We construct parallel EN/ZH conflict data from ConflictQA with COMET-validated translations, train per-layer logistic regression probes in four transfer directions, and apply three confound exclusion controls (COMET tercile ablation, token overlap analysis, and XNLI non-conflict baseline).}
\label{fig:pipeline}
\end{figure*}

These results carry two methodological implications.
The layer dissociation between probing peak and causal influence demonstrates that the layer with highest probe accuracy is not necessarily where the model resolves the conflict.
This challenges the common practice of intervening at the probing peak layer, consistent with the warning from \citet{basu2026interpretability} that detectability and causal relevance can diverge.
The directional asymmetry in cross-lingual transfer reflects a structural property of English-dominant multilingual models, not a conflict-specific phenomenon.
Any cross-lingual probing study must account for this baseline asymmetry to correctly interpret transfer differences.

Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Cross-lingual conflict detectability.} We provide the first evidence that knowledge conflict signals are linearly detectable across languages in residual stream representations, with all cross-lingual transfer directions exceeding chance (binomial $p < 0.001$).
    \item \textbf{Asymmetry reflects general cross-lingual structure.} The transfer asymmetry (ZH$\to$EN $>$ EN$\to$ZH by ${\sim}$7~pp) matches the XNLI non-conflict baseline in magnitude and direction, establishing that it reflects the model's general cross-lingual alignment rather than conflict-specific encoding.
    \item \textbf{Detection--decision dissociation in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.} Three independent signals---linear probe peak (L28), MLP probe peak (L18), and causal steering node (L13; Fisher $p = 0.002$)---diverge, demonstrating that linear detectability is neither sufficient nor predictive of causal relevance. Steering fails in Qwen and Gemma despite high probe accuracy, confirming this dissociation is not universal.
    \item \textbf{Confound exclusion pipeline.} We validate a pipeline of COMET translation quality ablation, token overlap analysis, and non-conflict baseline comparison that excludes common confounds in cross-lingual probing.
\end{itemize}

10	\paragraph{Why does steering fail in Qwen and Gemma?}
11	Three hypotheses merit consideration: (1)~non-linear causal interactions that single-direction perturbation cannot address \citep{elhage2022toy}; (2)~superposition with other features such that perturbing one direction disrupts unrelated computations \citep{templeton2024scaling}; (3)~architectural differences (e.g., Gemma's sandwich normalization) altering perturbation propagation.
12	
13	\paragraph{Preliminary hypothesis validation.}
14	Existing analyses address all three hypotheses.
15	For~(1), MLP probes gain $+9.2$~pp over linear probes on Llama conflict EN$\to$ZH but $-0.5$~pp on XNLI; Qwen shows a similar pattern ($+2.4$ vs.\ $-2.0$~pp), indicating conflict-specific non-linear encoding.

17	For~(3), Qwen and Gemma show mid-layer cross-task transfer dips (L14--L24) absent in Llama; L13 falls in Llama's dip-free region.
18	Definitive validation requires activation patching \citep{meng2022locating}.
